name: Margaret Whitlock
presenting_complaint: Worsening mid-thoracic back pain with new leg weakness and urinary retention

conditions: Metastatic breast cancer (bony metastases on prior imaging)
medical_history.social: Lives with husband. Independent with mobility until this week. Non-smoker.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 67-year-old woman with known metastatic breast cancer presents with 3 weeks of progressive mid-thoracic back pain, worse at night and on lying flat, now with 2 days of bilateral leg weakness, numbness from the umbilicus down, and today an inability to pass urine. She has not opened her bowels for 2 days. Obs are stable: BP 142/82, HR 88, afebrile, GCS 15. This is a neuro-oncological emergency until proven otherwise.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Back pain characterisation: 3 weeks progressive mid-thoracic pain, worse at night and lying flat, band-like/radicular radiation — classic malignant cord compression pattern (pain often precedes neurology, the warning window)
Red-flag neurology screen: bilateral leg weakness, ascending numbness, sensory level, gait disturbance, and NEW urinary retention / bowel dysfunction
Saddle/perineal anaesthesia and bladder/bowel symptoms specifically asked (cauda equina overlap) — new urinary retention and 2 days no bowel motion
Known metastatic breast cancer with bony metastases (high pre-test probability of metastatic spinal cord compression)
Analgesia history, anticoagulant use, and functional baseline (independently mobile until this week)
objective: Focused neuro exam of lower limbs: reduced power (e.g. bilateral 3/5 hip flexion/knee extension), documenting the level
Tone and reflexes: upper motor neuron signs below the lesion (increased tone, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars) in cord compression; flaccid/areflexic if cauda equina
Determine a SENSORY LEVEL to pinprick/light touch (e.g. sensory level at T10/umbilicus) and test SADDLE (perineal) sensation
Digital rectal exam for ANAL TONE and voluntary squeeze; assess bulbocavernosus reflex
Bladder assessment: palpable bladder and post-void residual via bladder scan / catheterisation (document residual volume, e.g. >500 mL confirming retention)
Palpate spine for level of bony tenderness; obs including temperature to help exclude epidural abscess
assessment: Metastatic (malignant) spinal cord compression until proven otherwise, given known metastatic breast cancer plus back pain with cord-level neurology
Cauda equina syndrome considered given urinary retention, bowel change and possible saddle anaesthesia — an emergency requiring urgent decompression
Differential: pathological vertebral fracture, spinal epidural abscess/haematoma, disc prolapse — but malignancy most likely here
Neurological deficit is time-critical: prognosis for recovery depends on speed of decompression before complete paraplegia
plan: Give high-dose corticosteroid NOW without waiting for imaging: dexamethasone 8-16 mg IV/oral stat (e.g. 16 mg) with PPI cover and BGL monitoring
Arrange URGENT whole-spine MRI immediately (whole spine to detect multi-level disease) — do not delay steroid for it, and do not delay the MRI
Urgent referral to neurosurgery/spinal surgery AND radiation oncology for emergency decompression or radiotherapy
Flat bed rest with spinal precautions/log-roll until spinal stability assessed
Insert urinary catheter for retention and document residual volume; commence bowel regimen; monitor for autonomic dysfunction
Analgesia: titrate opioids for severe pain (e.g. oxycodone/parenteral morphine), regular paracetamol; VTE prophylaxis (mechanical +/- pharmacological per surgical advice)
Bloods: FBC, UEC, calcium (hypercalcaemia of malignancy), LFTs, coagulation; and serial neurological observations to detect deterioration
Admit under joint oncology/neurosurgical care; document baseline neurology to track progression

critical_errors: Discharging/managing as simple mechanical back pain despite red flags (bilateral leg weakness, sensory level, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention, bowel change) in a patient with known malignancy
Delaying the urgent whole-spine MRI or emergency neurosurgical/oncology referral and decompression once cord compression is suspected
Waiting for imaging before giving the high-dose corticosteroid (dexamethasone should be given first when malignant cord compression is suspected)
Failing to recognise and relieve urinary retention (missed cauda equina bladder involvement / no catheter and no post-void residual documented)
must_not_miss: Malignant spinal cord compression / cauda equina syndrome requiring EMERGENCY decompression (surgery or radiotherapy)
Urinary retention identified and catheterised, saddle sensation and anal tone documented
High-dose dexamethasone given promptly and urgent whole-spine MRI arranged without delay
